503.name: *KTS Post Closing #35
503.subject: 10 tips for getting your furniture arrangement right
503.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

Like a blank page or canvas, an empty room can be either an opportunity or a challenge. With so many ways to fill it, how do you know where to start? An article in Houzz has taken some of the basic rules of furniture arrangement and distilled them into ten simple tips:

1. Think about how the room will function
Consider how many people will use the room. That will dictate the type of furnishings and amount of seating you'll need.

2. Decide on a focal point
Identify the room's focal point — a fireplace, view, television — and orient the furniture accordingly. If you plan to watch television in the room, the ideal distance between the set and the seating is three times the size of the screen (measured diagonally). So, if you've got a 40-inch set, your chair should be 120 inches away.

3. Start with priority pieces
Place the most significant pieces of furniture first, such as the sofa in the living room or the bed in the bedroom. In most cases, this piece should face the room's focal point. Chairs should be no more than eight feet apart to facilitate conversation. Unless your room is tiny, avoid pushing all the furniture against the walls.

4. Consider symmetry
Symmetrical arrangements work best for formal rooms, whereas asymmetrical arrangements make a room feel more casual.

5. Create a traffic flow
Think about the flow of traffic through the room — generally the path between doorways. Don't block that path with any large pieces of furniture if you can avoid it. Allow 30 to 48 inches of width for major traffic routes and a minimum of 24 inches for minor ones. Try to direct traffic around a seating group, not through the middle of it. If traffic cuts through the middle of the room, consider creating two small seating areas instead of one large one.

6. Aim for variety
Vary the size of furniture pieces throughout the room. Balance a large or tall item by placing another piece of similar height across the room from it (or use art to replicate the scale). Avoid putting two tall pieces next to each other.

7. Build in contrast
Combine straight and curved lines for contrast. If the furniture is modern and linear, add a round table for contrast. If the furniture is curvy, mix in an angular piece. Similarly, pair solids with voids: Combine a leggy chair with a solid side table and a solid chair with a leggy table.

8. Design for ease of use
Place a table within easy reach of every seat, be sure to combine pieces of similar scale, and make sure every reading chair has an accompanying lamp. Coffee tables should be located 14 to 18 inches from a sofa to provide sufficient legroom.

9. Allow for circulation
In a dining room, make sure there are at least 48 inches between each edge of the table and the nearest wall or piece of furniture. If traffic doesn't pass behind the chairs on one side of the table, 36 inches should suffice. In bedrooms, allow at least 24 inches between the side of the bed and a wall. And at least 36 inches between the bed and a swinging door.

10. Do your planning
Give your back a break. Before you move any furniture, test your design on paper. Measure the room's dimensions, noting the windows, doors, heat registers, and electrical outlets, then draw up a floor plan on graph paper using cutouts to represent the furnishings. Better yet, use a digital room planner to draw the space and test various furniture configurations. It's less work and a lot more fun.

I hope these tips come in handy for you!

Thanks,
#agent_name#

561.subject: The Power of Home Equity: How it Works and Benefits You
561.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

I wanted to share some insights into a topic that's important, but often misunderstood: home equity. I'm not sure if this is for you, but understanding home equity can open doors to significant financial benefits if you're a homeowner or plan to be one.

Simply put, home equity is the portion of your home that you truly own. It’s the difference between your home's market value and the outstanding balance of all liens on your property.

But here's the good news. Your home equity isn't static — it grows over time. Every time you make a mortgage payment, a portion goes towards reducing your loan balance, thereby increasing your equity. Your equity also grows if your home increases in value due to market conditions or home improvements.

Now, just imagine what could happen if you let this equity build up. Many homeowners leverage their home equity for large expenses like home improvements, education costs, money to go toward their next home, or even as a financial cushion for unexpected events.

However, before you make up your mind about using home equity, consider your options carefully. Borrowing against home equity can be useful, but it's important to remember that your home secures the loan. If you cannot make your loan payments, the value of your home could be at risk.

My role is to help you navigate your real estate journey and provide information that can assist you in making informed decisions. If you or someone you know is interested in discussing home equity or any other real estate topics, please feel free to reach out.

562.subject: Your Home's Year-Round Health: Maintenance Tips for Every Season
562.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

Today, I wanted to talk about something that we, as homeowners or future homeowners, can often overlook: seasonal home maintenance. I'm not sure if this is for you, but taking a proactive stance in maintaining your home through the seasons can lead to a more comfortable living environment and potentially even protect your home's value.

Spring:

Check Your Roof (if applicable): Winter can be tough on roofs. When spring arrives, check for any signs of damage, such as cracked or missing shingles, and have them repaired.

Clean Your Gutters (if applicable): Clear out any debris that's accumulated over winter. This ensures that spring rains can flow freely, avoiding water damage.

Service Your HVAC: Prepare your air conditioning system for warmer weather. It's a good idea to have it inspected by a professional.

Summer:

Check Your Outdoor Spaces (if applicable): Inspect your deck or patio for potential safety hazards like loose boards or protruding nails.

Service Your Sprinklers (if applicable): If you have a sprinkler system, make sure it's working properly so that your lawn stays lush throughout the summer months.

Inspect Your Windows and Doors: Check for any gaps that could let hot air in and cool air out. Sealing these can help your air conditioner run more efficiently.

Fall:

Prepare for Leaves (if applicable): Empty your gutters and downspouts and ensure they're prepared for the influx of falling leaves.

Check Your Heating System: Just as you serviced your air conditioning in the spring, it's time to ensure your heating is ready for the cold months.

Winterize Your Sprinkler System (if applicable): To avoid freezing and damage, make sure to drain and winterize your sprinkler system.

Winter:

Insulate Your Home: Ensure your home is adequately insulated to maintain a comfortable indoor temperature and reduce energy costs.

Check Your Smoke Detectors: With the increased use of heating systems and fireplaces in the winter, it's crucial to make sure your smoke detectors are working properly.

Protect Your Pipes: To prevent them from freezing and potentially bursting, insulate your pipes.

Don't worry if you feel like you can't do it all on your own. Many tasks can be handled by professionals who can ensure they're done right. If you need any recommendations for local service providers, I'm here to help.

Hi #lead_first_name#,

Today, I'd like to explore a topic that could potentially be a game-changer in your financial journey: real estate investing. I'm not sure if this is for you, but it could offer an exciting opportunity to diversify your investment portfolio and potentially create an additional income stream.

Becoming a real estate investor involves purchasing property with the intention of making a profit. This can be done through rental income, the resale of property in the future, or both.

You have 3 options when it comes to real estate investing:

Buying and Holding: This long-term investment strategy involves purchasing and renting a property out to tenants, generating a steady income over time. Just imagine the potential for consistent cash flow and the possibility of property value appreciation over time.

Flipping Properties: This short-term strategy involves buying a property, often needing repairs, renovating it, and selling it at a profit. While the potential for quick profits can be appealing, this approach often involves more risk and requires a deeper understanding of the property market.

Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs): These are companies that own or finance income-producing real estate. By investing in a REIT, you can potentially earn a share of the income produced through real estate investment without actually having to go out and buy, manage, or finance property.

If you're considering the path of investing, it's important to conduct thorough research and consider seeking advice from real estate and financial professionals.

566.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

I'm writing to you today to delve a little deeper into a topic we brushed upon in the previous email: real estate investing. But this time, I'd like to specifically focus on the debate between short-term and long-term rentals.

Investing in rental properties can be an effective way to generate income and build wealth, but the path you choose — short-term or long-term — depends on various factors. I'm not sure if this is for you, but I thought you or someone you know might find it useful.

Let's break down the basics:

Short-term Rentals:

These are properties that are rented out for short periods, typically on platforms like Airbnb or Vrbo.

Pros: The ability to charge higher nightly rates compared to a long-term lease can lead to a higher potential return on investment. It also offers flexibility if you want to use the property yourself.

Cons: The main downsides are the increased involvement and time needed to manage bookings, cleaning, and maintenance. Additionally, income can be more unpredictable due to seasonal demand fluctuations and market volatility.

Long-term Rentals:

These are properties that are leased out for longer periods, typically six months to a year or more.

Pros: One of the main advantages is the potential for a stable, consistent income stream. It also generally requires less hands-on management once a reliable tenant is in place.

Cons: On the downside, you may not be able to charge as much as a short-term rental, and you could encounter challenges if you end up with difficult tenants. There is also the commitment to a lease agreement, which might limit your flexibility.

Both paths have pros and cons, and what works best largely depends on your personal circumstances, investment goals, and the time you're willing to commit.

How important is it for you to create an additional income stream? How would you feel if you could achieve this through real estate investing? Most people find the prospect quite exciting.

Just out of curiosity, which investment strategy sounds more appealing to you?

Hi #lead_first_name#,

There are two types of people: those who diligently maintain their properties, ensuring they remain in excellent condition, and those who, unfortunately, allow their properties to decline over time, often leading to unexpected issues and compromising safety.

As a real estate professional, I frequently ask, "How often should I get my home inspected?" I bet you're a bit like me, curious and always seeking to be proactive, so I thought it would be helpful to discuss this topic today.

A home is one of the largest investments most people make in their lifetime. Therefore, it's essential to maintain it well. Regular home inspections can help identify potential issues before they become significant problems.

Most people only think about home inspections when buying or selling a property. But have you ever considered having a routine inspection even when a sale isn't on the horizon? It could be a wise move.

Here's a general rule of thumb: Consider having a professional inspect your home every 3–5 years. The good news is that regular inspections can help you catch potential issues early, saving you money and hassle in the long run.

Just imagine identifying a small leak before it causes significant damage or catching a minor electrical issue before it leads to a costly repair. These are just a couple of examples of the problems that a routine inspection can uncover.

Now, if you're considering an inspection, here's one more thing to note. An inspection doesn't just have to be for your entire home. If you have specific concerns — like the roof or HVAC system — you could have just that part of your home inspected.

Hi #lead_first_name#,

If you're using a mortgage to finance your new home, it's essential to keep certain things in mind after you've applied to ensure the process goes smoothly. Here are a few important tips:

Don't Change Bank Accounts: Keeping your financial situation consistent is crucial during the mortgage process. Changing banks could complicate the verification of your funds and financial history.

Avoid Applying for New Credit or Closing Existing Accounts: Any changes in your credit can impact your credit score, which lenders use to determine your eligibility and interest rate. Opening new credit lines or closing old ones can affect your debt-to-income ratio.

Hold Off on Large Purchases: Now might not be the time to buy a new car or expensive furniture. Large expenditures can affect your loan qualification by altering your financial profile.

Consult Before Depositing Large Sums of Cash: Large deposits need to be documented and explained to lenders. Before depositing any unusual amounts, discuss the implications with your bank or lender.

Refrain from Co-signing Loans: Co-signing could affect your credit and obligations, making it more challenging to secure your mortgage.

Discuss Any Financial Changes: If there are any changes in your income, assets, or financial plans, it’s best to discuss them with your lender to avoid any issues with your mortgage application.

Maintaining open communication with your lender and ensuring your financial profile remains stable can make a significant difference in the success of your mortgage application.

644.subject: 10 major red flags to watch for when home hunting
644.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

Buying a home is a significant decision, and it's essential to be vigilant. Here are critical red flags to watch for during your search:

Red Flag No. 1: Overpowering Scents
Be wary if you're greeted by strong fragrances like fresh-baked cookies or mulling spices. This could indicate an attempt to mask underlying odors.

Red Flag No. 2: Subpar Tiling
Check the tiling in kitchens and bathrooms. Poor workmanship might suggest quick fixes rather than proper repairs, potentially leading to significant future expenses.

Red Flag No. 3: Foundation Issues
While minor cracks are normal as homes settle, large gaps or misaligned doors and windows can indicate serious foundation problems.

Red Flag No. 4: Deferred Maintenance
Obvious maintenance neglect, like unattended roofs or outdated caulking, could signal more hidden problems, possibly revealed during a detailed home inspection.

Red Flag No. 5: Proximity to Water
A picturesque creek can become a risk if it threatens to flood your property.

Red Flag No. 6: Problematic Windows
Inspect windows for uneven frames and check if they open smoothly. Difficulty operating windows may also hint at foundation troubles or poor installation.

Red Flag No. 7: Mold Signs
Look for potential mold around bathroom cabinets and under sinks, especially near plumbing.

Red Flag No. 8: Water Damage
A musty smell can be a sign of hidden water damage, even without visible leaks.

Red Flag No. 9: Cosmetic Concealments
A newly painted wall could be covering something undesirable, like mold.

Red Flag No. 10: Inadequate Ventilation
Poor ventilation can lead to moisture buildup, visible through condensation on windows or bubbling paint, which is a precursor to mold growth.

Please reach out if you have any questions or need further guidance.

645.name: *KTS Active Buyer #8
645.subject: What are closing costs?
645.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,


As you prepare to buy a home, understanding the associated closing costs is vital.

Closing Costs Overview:
Closing costs are the various fees and expenses you pay to finalize the ownership of a home, which typically range from 2% to 5% of your mortgage loan amount (if you are getting a loan). These can include:

Origination Fee: Charged by your lender to begin the loan application.
Underwriting Fee: Paid to your lender for processing the application.
Appraisal Fee: Paid to assess the property's value, ensuring the purchase price is fair and the mortgage is appropriate.
Credit Report Fee: Covers the cost of checking your credit history.
Title Search Fee: Ensures the seller legally owns the property and can transfer ownership to you.
Recording Fees: Paid to the local municipality to officially record the property transaction.
Transfer Taxes: Paid to government entities involved in the transfer of the property.

Some buyers choose a no-closing-cost mortgage, where these fees are rolled into the loan, avoiding upfront payments but potentially increasing the loan’s interest.

How Long Does It Take to Close on a Home?
The closing process varies by the type of financing:

Conventional Loan: Average of 48 days.
FHA Loan: Average of 50 days.
VA Loan: Average of 56 days.
Cash Buyers: Typically, cash transactions can close quicker, often within 14 to 30 days, since they require fewer steps such as loan origination and underwriting.

Understanding these elements can help you plan better as you move forward in purchasing your new home.

Thanks,
#agent_name#

646.name: *KTS Active Buyer #9
646.subject: What you need to know about title
646.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

Every real estate transaction leaves a legal paper trail. When a property is sold, legal ownership is transferred through what's known as a title, in a process called a title transfer.

When you take title on your new home, there are several ways ownership can be structured. Each option has different legal and tax implications, so it’s important to consult with an attorney or CPA to decide what’s right for you.

Here are a few common forms of title vesting:

Tenancy in Common – Two or more individuals each hold an individual interest in the property. Interests may be equal or unequal, and each owner can sell or transfer their portion independently.

Joint Tenancy – Two or more individuals hold equal ownership rights. If one owner passes away, their share automatically transfers to the surviving owner(s).

Community Property – In certain states, married couples may own property jointly as community property. Both spouses share equal interest and must agree to any sale or transfer.

Sole Ownership – One individual holds the title alone. This can also apply to a married person who owns property separately from their spouse.

Your real estate agent can help guide the conversation and coordinate with professionals to ensure everything is handled correctly.

If you have any questions about title or ownership structure, feel free to reach out—I'm happy to help.

Thanks,
#agent_name#

648.subject: What is a closing statement?
648.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

As you prepare for your real estate closing, it's important to understand the closing statement, also known as a HUD-1 statement or settlement sheet. Here's some information you might find helpful:

A Closer Look
The closing statement is prepared by a closing agent and provides a detailed list of all expenses the buyer and seller must pay to complete the transaction. It includes:
  • Payments to agents
  • Mortgage insurance
  • Property tax deposits
  • Loan origination costs
  • Appraisal costs
  • Inspection costs
  • Mortgage broker fees
  • Borrower’s credit report costs
  • Escrow funds
  • Title search costs
  • Legal fees, including those for lawyers, notaries, and closing agents
Even after the statement is prepared, it may include last-minute changes that both parties need to review for accuracy. Costs are listed in two columns: the left side for the buyer’s expenses and the right for the seller’s expenses. The cash amount the buyer must give the seller is itemized at the bottom.

Both the buyer and seller should receive the closing statement at least one day before the transaction is completed, although it may sometimes be available only a few hours before closing. This statement provides a detailed record of all payments required to complete the transaction, allowing both parties to understand where the money is going and how much they’re spending.

650.subject: How to get over losing out on a home

Hi #lead_first_name#,

It isn't uncommon to experience "the home that got away syndrome."

So how do you cope when your supposed "chosen one" doesn't work out for whatever reason? Here are three tips to help you get through it:

Tip 1: Don't pretend it was no big deal. 
Don't hold that nasty stuff in. Let yourself feel everything – the disappointment, frustration, and the empty feeling of wondering what might have been. Allowing yourself to feel is the first step in working through difficult times.

Tip 2: Set new goals
Try to widen your perspective so you'll understand what worked and what can be improved, and set new goals with those lessons in mind. Was your dream home too far out of your budget? Did you go too low? Did you move on it too slowly? Is it possible to live with two bedrooms instead of three? Do you really want to live in that hot neighborhood, or perhaps you're willing to move farther away from the city? Would you be willing to take a second look at your list of wants vs. must-haves? What can you do differently next time?

Tip 3: Prepare to get back in the game
While it can be tough to forget about losing out on what you thought was your dream home, remember that many homes are still out there. It's best to consider what happened a learning experience and start looking at other properties again.

651.name: *KTS Active Buyer #13
651.subject: What usually comes with a home when you buy it
651.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

As you’re touring properties, you'll discover that some items won’t stay with a home while others will. In most purchasing contracts, it’s clear that anything built-in or permanently affixed comes with the home. This may seem like common sense, but you’d be surprised how many sellers assume they can take anything with them. Here is a list of what comes with a home in a typical contract:

Built-ins
Anything that’s built-in, such as built-in bookshelves, window seats, and cabinets, comes with the home.
Built-in outdoor cooking equipment: Does the home have a built-in outdoor grill, oven, or kitchen area? Since this is attached to the property, it typically comes with the home.

Outdoor items
Above-ground pools: These are typically included in the purchase of a home. If the buyer wants the pool disassembled, they may try to negotiate with the seller to get them to pay part of the cost.
Mailboxes: Whether streetside or wall-mounted, sellers will always leave a home’s mailbox.
Landscaping: Trees, shrubbery, and other landscaping planted in the ground come with the home. (Potted plants typically don’t.)
Pool equipment: While pool accessories (toys, tubes, etc.) don’t come with the home, pool equipment typically does.

Appliances
Range and oven: While some appliances do not automatically come with the home, built-in ranges and ovens always do.
Dishwasher: The majority of sellers include the dishwasher with the home purchase.
HVAC units: These are part of the home and are always included in the home purchase.

Lighting, decor, and accents
Ceiling fans: Ceiling fans are attached to the home and, therefore, stay with the home.
Pendants, chandeliers, and other light fixtures: Light fixtures that are affixed come with the home. If they are particularly expensive, the sellers usually work this cost into the home price.
Drapery rods, blinds, and window treatments: Since these are usually installed and attached to the home, they typically come with it.
All installed hardware: Most hardware comes with the home, including doorknobs, cabinet pulls and knobs, bathroom fixtures, etc.

Security and safety items
Smoke detectors: Sellers should always leave the smoke detectors when selling a home. As soon as buyers move in, we recommend checking the batteries to ensure they are working correctly.
Garage door openers and other access devices: Sellers always leave any access devices or codes with the new owners, including garage door openers, gate openers, and any security device.

What items are sometimes included with the home?
These items are not typically included with a home purchase but may be, depending on the needs and wishes of the seller and negotiations with the buyer.

Appliances
Refrigerator: Most buyers have seen a home without a refrigerator while home hunting, and that's because sellers usually have the right to take the fridge. This is almost always true of additional fridges, such as one kept in a garage. If the buyers want the refrigerator, they’ll usually have to specify that in the purchase agreement.
Freestanding microwaves: Countertop microwaves are not always included in a home purchase; these belong to the sellers and may be taken with them.
Washer and dryer: A home’s washer and dryer are not technically built-in, so they aren’t necessarily included in the home sale. Many buyers request the washer and dryer in their offer.

Recreational Items
Hot tub: A standalone hot tub doesn’t always come with the home. Many sellers will gladly include the spa in the home’s sale, given how challenging and expensive hot tubs are to move.

Decor
Mirrors: While bathroom mirrors usually come with the home, not all wall mirrors do. Double-check which mirrors stay and which mirrors go before buying a home.
Curtains and drapes: While built-in window treatments are included with a home, curtains and drapes can be an exception depending on the seller’s wishes.

Wall-mounted Items
TV mounting brackets: These are typically, but not always, left with the home. Buyers should check with the seller about whether or not they plan to leave the brackets installed in the walls.
Garage shelving or organizational systems: Any garage shelving or organizational system that isn’t built in doesn’t necessarily come with the home.

What doesn’t come with the home?
These items are rarely included in the purchase of a home, although they are sometimes purchased by the buyers separately.

Indoor and outdoor furniture: Not included, unless the sellers are open to selling their furniture. In that case, buyers may purchase furnishings from the sellers separately or as part of the purchase agreement.
TVs: Televisions (even those affixed to wall-mounted brackets) do not typically come with a home.

653.name: *KTS Active Buyer #15
653.subject: How's your home hunting etiquette?
653.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

When searching for your future home, it’s important to follow certain etiquette guidelines during the viewing process. Here are some suggestions for what to do and what to avoid when visiting someone’s home:

Do: Arrive on Time
First impressions matter, so start off right with the seller or listing broker by arriving on time. You might be putting in an offer on this home.

Do: Take Your Shoes Off
It’s courteous to remove your shoes at the door. Some sellers from different cultures may also require this.

Do: Ask Questions
Feel free to ask relevant questions about the home or surrounding community. While viewing the home, it’s acceptable to open:
  • Closets
  • Kitchen cabinets
  • Bedroom doors
  • Bathroom doors
  • Pantries
  • Linen closets
  • Dishwasher door (if staying with the home)
  • Refrigerator/freezer doors (if staying with the home)
  • Washer/dryer doors (if staying with the home)
If these are part of your decision-making process, it’s okay to want to view them. When in doubt, just ask! The seller or listing broker will likely allow it.

However, it is unacceptable to open:
  • Dressers
  • Nightstand drawers
  • Medicine cabinets
  • Laundry hampers/baskets
Sellers may leave written requests for what they prefer not to be viewed during showings, like private areas or anything containing personal information. Always respect the seller’s wishes. If you proceed with the purchase, you can view these areas during the home inspection.

Don’t: Use the Bathroom
Avoid using the bathroom during a showing unless it’s an emergency. Some sellers may be uncomfortable with this, especially if the home is vacant and clean.

However, if you’re considering buying the home, you may want to check the plumbing. With the seller's or listing broker's permission, it’s acceptable to test the plumbing for any issues.

Don’t: Bring Food
It’s impolite to bring food to a home showing, so leave snacks in the car. Sometimes, a seller or broker may offer refreshments to potential buyers.

Don’t: Negotiate While in the Home
The showing isn’t the time to discuss negotiations or point out every flaw. Wait until you’ve left to discuss your findings and opinions.

Don’t: Bring Kids or Pets
Bringing kids may require your attention and cause distractions. They might accidentally open certain drawers or cabinets. Similarly, leave pets at home while viewing a property.

As always, feel free to reach out to me if you have any questions.

Thanks,

654.name: *KTS Active Buyer #16
654.subject: Tips for writing a great offer
654.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

As we continue your property search, here are some helpful tips for writing a compelling offer:
  1. Write a Friendly Offer. Avoid including demands in your offer that could upset the seller. If most buyers request possession at 5 p.m. on the closing day, stand out by giving the seller a few extra days to move out.
  2. Put Your Best Foot Forward. Submit your very best offer. You may only get one chance to impress the seller, so avoid making a low offer with the hope of a counteroffer. If the seller has multiple offers, low ones are often disregarded. Determine the top dollar you’re willing to pay and offer that amount.
  3. Put Down a Healthy Earnest Money Deposit. A larger earnest money deposit demonstrates seriousness and commitment. Sellers feel more confident with a 3% deposit compared to a 1% deposit. 
  4. Cash Talks. If you can pay cash, let the seller know. Although the seller receives cash even if the buyer has a mortgage, stating you’re paying cash shows your offer isn't dependent on loan approval, making you a more attractive buyer.
  5. Shorten Inspection Periods. Real estate purchase contracts often allow buyers a certain number of days for inspections. If the standard period is 17 days, consider reducing it to 10 days. This is a great way to stand out on paper, while not costing you a dime out of pocket.
  6. Waive Contingencies. Talk with me before waiving contingencies, such as loans, appraisals, or inspections. If you waive an appraisal contingency and the home appraises below the sale price, you’ll need to cover the difference in cash. While waiving contingencies has risks, it can make your offer more appealing than a competitor’s.
  7. Offer to Close Quickly. Many sellers prefer closing within 30 days or less. Offering a 21-day closing timeframe (or as quick as your lender can complete the loan), might give you an edge over the competition. For some sellers, a quick closing can be more important than a higher offer.

655.subject: What is title insurance and why is it necessary?
655.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

Title insurance is a unique type of insurance that protects against issues with the legal ownership of a property. It covers potential problems like unknown liens, errors in public records, or past ownership claims that could surface after your purchase.

In most transactions, two types of title insurance policies are involved:

  • A lender’s policy, which protects the lender’s interest in the property and is usually required when there’s a mortgage. This cost is typically part of the buyer’s closing expenses.
  • An owner’s policy, which protects the buyer’s interest in the property. While customs vary by region, this policy is often included in the transaction—sometimes paid for by the seller, sometimes negotiated as part of the offer.
While specifics can differ depending on the terms of the contract, title insurance is a common part of the home buying process and offers important peace of mind. It helps ensure that when you close on your new home, no one else can claim a right to it.

If you’d like help understanding how it works in your area, just reply—I’m happy to walk you through it.

  2. Change the Locks. You don’t know how many people have keys to your new home from the previous owner. Call a locksmith to change the locks for added security.

669.name: *KTS Pending Buyer #8
669.subject: Which closing documents should be kept?
669.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

When you close on a home, you'll sign a substantial number of documents. While you may not have room to store all of this paperwork, it's important to maintain a complete file. Make sure to keep copies of all documents signed during the transaction from start to finish.

Preliminary Documents
  • Buyer’s Agent Agreement. This contract outlines the terms of your relationship with your real estate agent’s brokerage, including the duration of the agreement and termination conditions. It's crucial to keep a copy for future reference, as issues may arise after the sale.
  • Purchase Agreement. This contract details all terms and conditions for buying the home. It's the agreement you and the seller signed, legally obligating both parties to its terms.
Documents Leading Up to Closing
  • Addendums, Amendments, or Riders. These documents modify or clarify your original purchase contract, such as name spellings or street addresses.
  • Requests for Repair. These documents outline any monetary agreements or repairs, potentially serving as addendums to the purchase agreement. They specify required work, permits, and whether a licensed contractor must complete it.
  • Seller Disclosures. These documents disclose material facts about the property, such as lead-based paint. They can include transfer disclosure statements, warranties, and guarantees. Sellers may face future lawsuits if they fail to disclose issues.
Closing Documents
  • Home Inspection Summary. This report identifies items in good condition and those needing repair or replacement, often including photos. It can be used for negotiation and later as a repair checklist.
  • Pest Inspection and Completion Certificate. This document certifies completed work. Some states, like California, require this to be kept on file for two years.
  • Other Inspections and Work-Related Documents. These may include contractor invoices and permits.
  • Closing Disclosure. This document lists all final mortgage costs and is essential for tax time. Some items may be tax-deductible, so consult your tax preparer.
  • Closing Statement. Also known as the HUD-1 Settlement Statement, this document details the sale price, closing costs, loan amount, and credits. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau replaced it with the closing disclosure in 2015.
Insurance Documents
  • Home Warranty Plans. Include policy numbers and repair call contact information, outlining coverage details.
  • Insurance Policy. Covering terms, conditions, and premium information, this policy is required if your loan is impounded. Otherwise, you'll pay the premium annually, potentially included in your mortgage payment.
  • Title Insurance Policy. This document outlines coverage details, exceptions, and policy information, serving as a defense against previous liens.
Documents to Keep as Originals
  • Closing Disclosure. This official document details all home purchase charges and credits. It's needed for tax purposes as some items may be deductible.
  • Deed. This title transfer document, recorded by the county, proves ownership and includes the legal property description.
Thanks,

673.subject: How to be a home seller buyers love
673.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

Many people don't realize it but as a seller, how you conduct yourself through the sales process is extremely important to your potential buyer. They may like the home – but they probably won't go through with the purchase if they don't like who's selling it. Take note of the following seller guidelines:

1. Stay away.
Yes, it's still your home and you have every right to stay in it. But if you're trying to show it to potential new owners, you'll want to avoid hovering over their shoulders.

2. Make your parking space available.
When leaving the home for the viewing, take your car with you. Parking issues can cause delays and turn off buyers, so get off to a good start by making sure they have a place to park their car. Let them pull up in your driveway as if it's their own.

3. Don't leave your pets.
Your pets have to go, too – no matter how sweet and friendly they are. Some buyers may be allergic to certain animals, or just find pet smells off-putting. Some DO love animals, but you also don't want your pet to draw attention away from the home. Just take them with you during the viewing, or ask a kind neighbor to pet-sit.

4. Make important documents available for viewing.
Since you won't be there to answer questions yourself, make it easy for potential buyers to find the answers in writing. Having necessary documents available leaves a good impression on buyers, as it signals that you're a responsible owner and seller. Put out important documents such as your home inspection report, appraisal, and home warranty. You can also give potential buyers an idea of their potential monthly bills by leaving recent utility bills and proof of any major repairs.

5. Don't be in a hurry to get feedback.
Not all buyers express their dislike or enthusiasm during or immediately after the viewing. Some of them need to think it over and process everything they just saw. This is possibly one of the biggest purchases they'll ever make, and buyers need enough space and time to come up with an offer. Asking them for their feedback right after leaving your home can make them feel that you're pressuring them too much into a decision.

It is normal practice to ask for feedback from your realtor after the viewing, but expect to hear from the buyer's agent no earlier than two days. Assure them that you are patiently waiting for what they have to say and respect their space and time.

As always, don't hesitate to let me know if you have any questions.

674.name: *KTS Seller Listed #3
674.subject: How to avoid seller’s remorse
674.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

Seller's remorse is a real phenomenon – one that's very common.

To make sure you aren't plagued with feelings of regret later, take some time to examine the factors that cause seller’s remorse. From there, you can follow a plan to prevent it from popping up when it’s too late. Here are a few considerations:

1. Did I price my home right?
After the sale of their home, sellers may have second thoughts about the amount they sold it for. Some feel that they may have accepted an offer that was too low, especially if they didn't have any other offers.

How to prevent this situation: We did a fair amount of strategy together to price your home. I will keep an eye on market trends and showings to ensure you are priced correctly for the current market. 

2. Was it really the right time to sell?
It’s not unusual for sellers to make an impulsive decision to sell their homes just because the current market promises good returns. Some people also decide to sell to get out of debt, but realize that there could have been other ways to raise the money without giving up their homes.

How to prevent this situation: You have a solid and acceptable reason for selling your home. This helps you not to feel guilty about it in the end.

3. Will I be able to find a home that appeals to me as much as the one I just sold? (if applicable)
Sellers who have loved their previous home often worry if they’ll ever find a worthy replacement.

How to prevent this situation: It’s normal to feel an attachment to the home you’re selling, but if you’re worried that you won’t find a home you’ll love just as much – don’t panic. We have strategized and will continue to do so together for the perfect plan for you.

Encouragement for sellers
The bittersweet feeling of parting with your home is often inevitable, but a bad case of seller’s remorse is something you can avoid with careful planning. The anxiety brought on by having to sell a home you’ve loved for a long time will eventually be eased by having a positive outlook as you transition into this new phase in your life. Just remember to hire an agent you can trust and be 100 percent sure of your decision to sell.

Thanks,

The buyer's mortgage file goes to underwriting after all the buyer's supporting documents have been received by the lender and after an appraisal has been completed. 

The appraisal must support the agreed-upon purchase price. 

3. A contingent sale (if applicable)
A buyer might have to close escrow on an existing home before moving forward with purchasing the new home. This is known as a contingency sale, and the contingency must usually be satisfied or released to move forward with the contract.

678.name: *KTS Seller Pending #7
678.subject: Home-closing checklist tips for sellers
678.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

When selling your home, there are important tasks to address. Creating a home-selling checklist can help ensure you complete everything efficiently, even after your personal belongings and furniture are removed. While you might not be legally required to vacate immediately upon closing, here are key items to include in your checklist:

Secure Your Documents
Keep all seller disclosures, the purchase contract, and the closing statement together in one location. These documents might be needed later if any issues arise. Ideally, your escrow officer or real estate agent will provide a complete package at closing.

Cancel Your Insurance Policies
Wait until the deed has been recorded or the title transfer is complete before contacting your insurance agent. You should receive a refund for any prepaid homeowner’s insurance premiums.

Close Accounts
Prepare a list of contact numbers for each utility and entertainment company. Remember that some utilities aren’t paid monthly, so you may need to pay a balance, receive a refund, or transfer the balance to your new home.

Necessary Incidentals
Leave home keys, remotes, gate keys, pool keys, and mailbox keys for the new owners in an easily found location like a kitchen drawer. Assemble a packet with appliance manuals, receipts, and warranties for the HVAC, security system, sprinkler system, and appliances, and leave them with the security alarm code.

Don’t Leave Anything Behind
Check cabinets, drawers, and storage areas for forgotten items. Do a final check, even if someone else has already searched.

Lock Up on Your Way Out
Close blinds and lock windows and doors. This is crucial, especially if the home will be vacant. Consider leaving a lamp on a timer for added security.

Change Your Address
Notify everyone of your new address and submit a change-of-address form to the post office. Remember that not all mail is forwarded, so contact some entities directly.

680.name: *KTS Seller Pending #4
680.subject: From the outside in: What home appraisers look for
680.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

When appraisers evaluate a home, they consider several key factors. Here's what they typically look for:

Interior
  • Compliance with housing codes, including health and safety standards
  • Total square footage of bedrooms, bathrooms, and kitchens
  • Structural integrity and overall condition of the home
  • Functionality and condition of appliances and utilities
  • Efficiency and functionality of the layout
  • Condition of HVAC and plumbing systems
Exterior
  • Age of the home and construction quality
  • Condition of the roof, foundation, siding, and gutters
  • Location, neighborhood, and position of the property site
  • Condition of driveways and parking areas
As a home seller, you can provide the appraiser with additional information for a more accurate valuation, such as details about the property’s sale and rental history and any agreements with neighbors regarding fences, walls, or easements.

Additional Factors in Appraisal
Besides the physical features of the home, appraisers rely on market data from the surrounding area to prepare the appraisal. They research public records, consult with local real estate professionals about listings, sales, leases, land, and construction costs, and access the Multiple Listing Service (MLS) for real estate market insights.

Comparables
Comparables are crucial in determining the home's value. Recent sales or listings with similar features (age, size, location, amenities) help shape the final appraisal. If necessary, appraisers may interview agents with nearby listed properties.

After the Appraisal
After evaluating the home using various approaches, the appraiser compiles all the data, including comparables and inspection findings, to form a final opinion of value. The lender then receives the appraisal to decide if the loan amount aligns with the appraisal value.

Feel free to reach out if you have any questions about these items. I'm happy to help.

681.name: *KTS Seller Pending #6
681.subject: What stays with the home when you move?
681.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

When selling your home, you might think that anything you can safely remove is yours to keep, like the light fixtures you've meticulously maintained or the appliances you bought last year. However, buyers may also be interested in some of these items. It’s important to decide what you should leave behind to entice buyers into making an offer. Here are some tips:

What to Leave with the Home
  • Built-ins: Items like built-in bookshelves, benches, and pull-out furniture should stay.
  • Landscaping: Trees, shrubs, and flowers planted in the ground should remain.
  • Wall Mounts: Leave TV and picture mounts that could damage walls if removed.
  • Custom-fit Items: Custom-made curtains, plantation shutters, or blinds should stay.
  • Hardware: Leave upgraded knobs and drawer pulls or replace them before moving.
  • Alarm Systems: Leave alarm monitoring stations attached unless they're wireless.
  • Smoke Detectors: Smoke detectors and sprinkler systems should remain, especially if you move before selling.
What You Can Take
  • Outdoor Accessories: Patio furniture, lawn equipment, and playsets are yours to keep.
  • Appliances: While an oven may be required, other appliances can be taken or left as part of the sale.
  • Light Fixtures: You can arrange with the buyer to take specific fixtures, possibly providing replacements.
  • Built-in Kitchen Tools: Safely removable items like a mounted spice rack can be taken.
  • Rugs and Small Decor: Items like rugs and curtain rods that can be removed are yours to keep.
What to Consider Leaving
  • Appliances: Offering appliances can attract buyers, especially those without their own.
  • Playsets: If your children have outgrown a swing set or playhouse, consider offering it to buyers with children.
  • Kitchen Built-ins: Items like spice racks or pantry organizers can enhance your kitchen’s appeal.
  • Upgrades: Buyers may increase their offer to keep upgraded light fixtures, custom rugs, and other enhancements.
I hope you find this information helpful. As always, feel free to reach out with any questions or concerns.

682.name: *KTS Seller Pending #2
682.subject: Preparing for inspection
682.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

The buyer will be scheduling a property inspection soon. Here are some tips from professional home inspectors to help minimize issues and avoid any red flags that might give buyers the wrong impression:

  • Ensure Utilities Are On. Make sure gas, electricity, water, and other utilities are turned on so the inspector can complete their report.
  • Provide Access to All Areas. Check that the inspector can easily access all areas of the home, including the attic, crawlspace, garage, shed, and storage closet. Ensure nothing heavy is blocking access, and provide remote controls for any equipment being sold with the home, like lights, fireplaces, or ceiling fans.
  • Make Windows Accessible. Arrange furniture and window coverings so that windows are easily inspected. If the inspector cannot access certain areas, they may need to return for a second visit.
  • Consider Not Being Present. Inspections can take four to five hours, so plan accordingly. It's often best not to be present during the inspection.
  • Use a Checklist to Prepare
    • Outside:
    • Clean gutters and downspouts
    • Check wood trim joints for caulk and softness
    • Secure or replace loose wood or bricks on steps
    • Fix nail pops and loose shingles on the roof
    • Assess hose faucets for leaks
    • Inside:
    • Change air filters
    • Adjust doors that stick
    • Repair holes from door handles
    • Replace burned-out lightbulbs
    • Ensure all outlets have covers
    • Inspect the water heater for corrosion and leaks
    • Test the stove burners for functionality
    • Run the dishwasher and garbage disposal
    • Check that all toilets flush properly
    • Garage:
    • Move stored items away from walls to allow foundation inspection
    • Test the automatic reverse function and garage door opener
  • Don’t Leave Pets at Home. Ensure pets are not present during the inspection.
An inspection report is typically sent to the buyer(s) a few days after the inspection is completed.

I hope you find these tips helpful. As always, feel free to contact me if you have any questions.

683.name: *KTS Seller Pre-Listed #1
683.subject: Thank you for listing with me!
683.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

Thank you for trusting me with your listing. Our next steps involve scheduling the stager, professional photographer, videographer, and a property visit to take room measurements and install the lockbox. When you’re ready to schedule these visits, please let me know, and I’ll handle it. Meanwhile, here are some tips to help you prepare your property:

Depersonalize Your Home
Pack away personal photographs, family heirlooms, and other objects that might distract potential buyers. Presenting an impersonal, clean environment helps buyers imagine the home with their own decor and furnishings. Keep furniture understated to avoid creating unintended impressions. For example, it can be hard for buyers to picture their antique furnishings if there's a zebra couch or a bright yellow chair in place.

Declutter Your Home
People tend to collect a lot over the years for reasons such as emotional attachment or future use. However, if you haven’t used items in over a year, you likely don’t need them. Donate unwanted items to charities or nonprofit organizations like Goodwill, where they can help others and may be tax-deductible. For items not accepted, check with your town about pick-up services, often available once or twice a month.

Remove books and knickknacks from bookcases, and clear your kitchen counters. Tuck essential daily-use items into small boxes stored in a closet when not in use. Consider this a head start on your packing.

Make Minor Repairs
Fix leaky faucets, doors that don’t close properly, and jammed kitchen drawers. Paint walls in neutral colors if they’re currently bright or unconventional. Avoid giving buyers reasons to remember your home for unusual features, like an orange bathroom.
Replace burned-out lightbulbs and consider changing older ones to prevent them from blowing out during showings. Ensuring everything is in working order can make the buyer's experience more positive.

Make the Home Sparkle
Consider hiring a professional cleaning crew to prepare your home for viewings. Cleaning may include:
  • Washing windows inside and out
  • Pressure washing sidewalks and the exterior
  • Recaulking tubs, showers, and sinks
  • Polishing chrome faucets and mirrors
Remove dust from under furniture, inside cabinets, and closets. Maintain cleanliness by vacuuming, waxing floors, dusting furniture, and keeping bathrooms and kitchens spotless. Hang fresh guest towels, and keep toilet lids closed.

Kitchens are major selling points, so keep yours spotless and uncluttered. Ensure the refrigerator is clean and orderly.
Clean and air out musty areas, and avoid cooking odorous foods like fish, garlic, or cabbage the night before a showing. If you have pets, monitor litter boxes and any other affected areas.

689.name: *KTS Seller Pre-Listed #5
689.subject: Important repairs to make
689.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

As a savvy seller, you’ll want your home in excellent condition without overspending on improvements. The key is to focus on the most critical repairs that will support a higher asking price. Here are some essential repairs to consider:

  1. Repair Damaged Flooring. Scratched wood flooring, worn-out carpeting, and outdated linoleum can make your home seem neglected. These issues can quickly turn buyers away. Installing new flooring can significantly increase your home’s value.
  2. Fix Water Stains. Water stains, even from long-resolved plumbing issues, can suggest underlying problems to buyers. Fixing these stains is crucial before listing your home. Ensure any leaks are resolved by hiring a plumber, with potential costs around $300 for a leaking pipe. Repairing a water-stained ceiling costs about $670, and drywall repairs are approximately $1.50 per square foot—much cheaper than losing a sale.
  3. Repair Torn Window Screens. Repairing window screens is inexpensive and can be a DIY project. A repair kit from a home improvement store costs $10 to $15. Given the simplicity, making these fixes is worthwhile.
  4. Update Grout. Yellowing or cracked grout stands out to buyers, but new grout can make old floors look new. Simple re-grouting costs $1 to $2 per square foot, while more complex jobs might be $10 per square foot. If you’re handy, doing it yourself can save even more.
  5. Revive the Lawn. A brown, patchy lawn suggests maintenance issues. Fixing it is affordable and can yield a significant return when selling. Hiring a lawn care service for fertilizer and weed control costs about $375 but can boost your home’s value by $1,000—a 267% return on investment.
  6. Repair Pet Damage. Address any pet damage, like scratched doors or flooring. Refinishing a door costs between $100 and $215, while replacing damaged flooring is more involved but worth the expense.

690.name: *KTS Seller Pre-Listed #6
690.subject: Avoid these 8 home staging mistakes
690.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

Everyone makes mistakes, but some can turn off potential home buyers. Here are eight common home staging mistakes sellers often make—and how you can avoid them.

Mistake #1: Focusing on Trends
Is farmhouse decor still popular? What's the Pantone color of the year? Fortunately, these details don’t matter when staging your home to sell. While you want to impress buyers, focusing too much on popular design styles might alienate some. Your safest bet is a transitional style—one that’s neither too trendy nor too traditional.

Mistake #2: Overdoing Neutrals
Creating a light, airy, and neutral environment is important, but going too far can make your home feel bland and lifeless. Don’t be afraid to add some color. If you have a large living area with natural light and high ceilings, consider adding a focal wall to bring the space to life.

Mistake #3: Old Paint
Even if your walls are already neutral, a fresh coat of paint can make your home feel brand new to potential buyers. Don’t forget the ceiling—a fresh coat of white can do wonders.

Mistake #4: Dark, Gloomy Rooms
Lighting is key to showcasing your home. Here are some tips:
  • Remove heavy or dark window treatments. Opt for light, translucent curtains that accentuate windows without blocking light.
  • Ensure each room has at least four light sources, including lamps, recessed lights, and sconces.
  • Use cool LED lights instead of warm ones. Choose soft or warm LED white bulbs with about 3,000 Kelvins and at least 800 lumens. Consistency is important—make sure all bulbs are the same to create a cohesive look.
Mistake #5: Poor Furniture Placement
We often push furniture against walls, but look at any room you admire online. Notice how furniture sits a few feet from the walls, allowing light to flow and creating walkways.

Mistake #6: Oversized Furniture
A large couch, even if it fits your style, can make a room look smaller. Choose appropriately sized furniture to make spaces feel open and inviting.

Mistake #7: Ignoring Outdoor Spaces
Imagine dressing up for a gala but neglecting your hair. A neglected yard can ruin the effect of your beautifully staged interior. Ensure your outdoor spaces are well-maintained to complement your home’s interior appeal.

Mistake #8: Neglecting Cleanliness
No one appreciates a well-designed room if it’s dusty or has stained carpets. Clean thoroughly, including organizing the garage and removing oil stains. Pay special attention to the entryway to make a strong first impression.

Remember, your home has served you well, so give it the attention it deserves before moving on. You’ve been on the other side, judging which listings are worth visiting. Make sure your home stands out by avoiding these common pitfalls.

Thanks,
#agent_name#

691.name: *KTS Seller Pre-Listed #7
691.subject: Common costs associated with selling your home
691.body:
Hi #lead_first_name#,

Closing costs for real estate sellers can vary depending on your location. These costs are usually deducted from your home’s profit. Here’s an overview of typical costs included in seller closing costs:

1. Real Estate Commissions

Traditionally, one of the largest closing costs for sellers has been the commission paid to the real estate agents involved in the transaction. This amount has typically been split between the listing agent and the buyer’s agent.
However, following changes in industry practices and recent legal settlements, this model is evolving. Commissions remain negotiable, and buyers may now be responsible for compensating their own agent directly—rather than the seller covering both sides by default.

That said, it’s still very common for buyers to request that the seller cover their agent’s fee as part of the offer, often by factoring it into the purchase price. So while the path may look different, the end result often resembles the way things have traditionally been handled.

What this means for you:
If you’re selling a home, it’s more important than ever to understand how commissions are structured in your market, what’s being asked of you in the offer, and how that affects your bottom line.

2. Loan Payoff Costs
Your mortgage payoff balance might be slightly higher than your remaining mortgage balance and the buyer’s purchase price due to prorated interest.

In some cases, your lender may charge a prepayment penalty for early payoff. If you have a home equity loan or line of credit, it will need to be paid in full at closing. Consult your lender to get a clear picture of these costs.

3. Transfer Taxes or Recording Costs
Transfer taxes and recording fees are standard costs associated with transferring ownership of a property and are typically set by your state or local government. These fees vary by location and are part of the closing process.

Property taxes also play a key role at closing. If your property taxes are paid and current, you'll typically receive a credit for the portion of the year you won’t own the home—prorated based on the closing date. If you haven’t yet paid your current taxes, that amount will usually be debited from your proceeds at closing, again prorated from the date of transfer.

Understanding how these prorations work can help you avoid surprises on your final closing statement.


4. Title Insurance Costs
Title insurance protects the buyer and lender against title problems. Sellers usually pay for the owners title insurance policy, while the buyer foots the bill for any lender mandated title policy for the loan

Additional costs may include:
  • Liens or judgments against the property
  • Unpaid homeowners association dues
  • Prorated property taxes and HOA dues up to the closing date
Depending on the real estate contract, closing costs might also include:
  • Termite inspection and clearance, if needed
  • Home warranty premium for buyers
  • Repair costs or credits for items mutually agreed upon during the transaction
